## Part 0 — Before the Cartographer
### *The four crossings that almost worked, and why the fifth one changed everything*

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Four panels: ELIZA (1966), n-grams (1990s), RNN/LSTM (2010s), Transformer (2017)." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 2 — Four predecessors. Each one walked a little farther into the desert than the last; each one collapsed in a different way. The Transformer was built from the exact shape of the gaps they left.*

Before we hand the cartographer their journal and watch them step into the sand, we need to look at the bones in the dunes. The Transformer did not appear out of nowhere in 2017. It was the **fifth attempt** at the same crossing, and every part of its design is a direct response to the specific way the previous four had died. **You will understand attention infinitely better once you have felt the ache the previous architectures could not soothe.**

### The First Crossing — ELIZA (1966)

The first cartographer carried no map at all. **ELIZA** was a pattern-matcher: if the input contained the word *"mother"*, the output was a canned reply about your family. There was no representation of meaning, no memory, no learning — just a rulebook. It felt like conversation because humans are generous interpreters, not because ELIZA had any idea what it was doing.

**The ache it left:** *we need a model that actually represents the input, not just matches it.*

### The Second Crossing — n-grams (1990s)

The next cartographer carried a **fixed-size window** of the last *n* footprints — usually 3, sometimes 5. To predict the next word, they looked only at the last 2–4 words and asked: *"what usually comes after this exact sequence in my training data?"*

This worked surprisingly well for short, common phrases. But the model could not see further back than its window. Anything more than 4 words ago might as well have never happened. And as you grew the window, the number of possible sequences exploded combinatorially, so you needed exponentially more training data to estimate the probabilities reliably.

**The ache it left:** *we need a model whose memory of the past doesn't have a hard cliff at n tokens, and whose statistics don't explode.*

### The Third Crossing — RNNs, LSTMs, and the Sequence-to-Sequence Postcard (2014)

This is the crossing the original document mentioned in passing. It deserves more than a footnote, because **the entire shape of the Transformer is a response to exactly how this crossing failed.** So we will walk it slowly.

#### First, the leather notebook

The third cartographer carried a small **leather notebook in their pocket**. As they walked the desert and saw each footprint (each input token), they updated the notebook with a *running summary of everything they had seen so far*. The notebook had a fixed number of pages — say 512 — and every step they re-wrote those pages to incorporate the latest observation, while also dragging forward what they could from the previous summary.

That leather notebook is what the literature calls a **hidden state**, and the cartographer is what we call a **Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)** — or, in its better-engineered form, an **LSTM** (long short-term memory) which added a clever gating mechanism to decide what to keep, what to forget, and what to write down fresh at each step.

The hidden state was finite. The desert was not. That was the first crack.

#### Then, the two cartographers

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Two cartographers separated by a vertical channel: one walks the input desert and mails a glowing postcard to a second cartographer who waits in an empty output desert." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 3 — The Seq2Seq setup. An encoder cartographer walks the input desert and mails a single fixed-size postcard. A decoder cartographer in the output desert must paint the full translation from that postcard alone, one footprint at a time.*

In 2014 a beautiful idea appeared: what if we used **two cartographers**, working two different deserts?

Imagine you want to translate *"I love machine learning"* into French. The first cartographer — the **encoder** — walks the English desert, footprint by footprint, updating their leather notebook the whole way. At the last word, they stop, close the notebook, and **mail its final page** as a single fixed-size sheet of paper to a second cartographer waiting in an empty French desert. That sheet is the only thing the second cartographer will ever see of the English input.

The second cartographer — the **decoder** — receives that single page and begins to walk their own desert, **one footprint at a time**, pressing French words into the sand: *J'aime*, then *l'apprentissage*, then *automatique*. They look at the postcard and at the footprints they have already pressed, predict the next one, press it, and repeat until they press the *end-of-desert* marker.

That entire choreography is called a **sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) model**, and it was the first architecture in the world that could take a variable-length input and produce a variable-length output *of a different format* — translation, summarization, question-answering. It was a real conceptual breakthrough.

#### The postcard has a name: the context vector

That single sheet of paper mailed between cartographers has a name in the literature: **the context vector**. And the most important fact about it — the one that decided the entire fate of seq2seq — is this:

> **The postcard is always the same size, no matter how big the desert was.**

If the encoder's hidden state has dimension 512, the context vector is 512 numbers. **Always 512 numbers.** Whether the input was *"hi"* (two tokens) or the entire opening chapter of *War and Peace* (3,000 tokens), the encoder closes its notebook at the end and what gets mailed is the same fixed-size page.

Why fixed-size? Because the architecture demanded it. RNNs produce one hidden state per step, each of dimension *d* baked into the encoder's wiring at design time. The convention was simply: **the encoder's final hidden state *is* the context vector.** There was no mechanism to "grow the postcard" if the desert got longer.

Now think about what that means for *War and Peace*. The cartographer who walked all three thousand footprints arrives at the mailbox exhausted, and what they remember most vividly is the **last few footprints they pressed**. Everything from the early chapters has been overwritten by 3,000 successive updates to the same 512-page notebook. By the time the postcard is sealed, Natasha and Pierre are ghosts and only the final battle is legible.

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A long trail of footprints funnels into a small cracked postcard; on the right, a faded trail of output footprints emerges." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 4 — The postcard bottleneck. When the input desert is long, the fixed-size context vector cannot hold it all. Information from the earliest footprints gets smeared by the latest ones, and the decoder receives a postcard that already lost the first half of the message.*

#### The second cartographer walks one footprint at a time

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A trail of output footprints with red feedback arcs from each footprint to the next, and a postcard above broadcasting to every step." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 5 — Autoregressive decoding. Every new footprint depends on (a) the postcard and (b) every footprint already pressed. The red arcs are the feedback loop; the dotted gold lines are the postcard broadcast.*

The decoder cannot paint the French desert all at once. It has to paint it **one footprint at a time**, and each new footprint depends on two things:

1. **The postcard** (the fixed context vector from the encoder).
2. **Every footprint the decoder has already pressed.**

That second condition has a name: it is what makes the model **autoregressive**. The decoder is *regressing on its own past output.* In probability terms, it factorizes the joint probability of the entire output sequence as a product of one-token-at-a-time predictions:

$$P(y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_T \mid x) \;=\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} \; P(y_t \mid y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1},\; x)$$

In cartographer-speak: at footprint *t*, the decoder asks **"given the postcard and the footprints I've already pressed, what's the most likely next footprint?"** It samples one, presses it, and asks the same question again — now with one more footprint in its history. The loop runs until the model presses the *end-of-desert* marker, `<EOS>`.

**Why must generation be autoregressive?** Because natural language has dependencies. You cannot choose *"automatique"* until you already wrote *"l'apprentissage"* — *"automatique"* is the feminine adjective form that agrees with *"l'apprentissage"*. If you tried to predict every output token in parallel from just the postcard, you would get grammatical confetti.

And here is the crucial point that survives the fall of every previous architecture: **this autoregressive idea never went away.** GPT, Claude, Llama, every modern decoder-only LLM is still doing exactly this. They still predict the next token from the previous tokens, press it, and loop. **What changed was *what they get to look at when predicting each token.*** The seq2seq decoder looked at the postcard plus its own history. The Transformer decoder looks at *every previous token directly* — no postcard required.

#### Why the third crossing died

We can now name the ache precisely. Seq2Seq failed for two specific reasons, both visible in Figure 4:

1. **The postcard bottleneck.** No matter how rich the input desert, the entire crossing had to fit on a fixed-size sheet. Information was lost. Long sentences translated badly because the early words were crushed by the late words. The decoder simply never received them.

2. **Sequential generation was slow and forgetful.** The encoder had to process tokens one at a time (you cannot compute the 100th hidden state until the 99th is done), so training could not be parallelized across the input. And the decoder, generating its own output, could only carry one hidden state forward — by the 50th French word, its memory of the 1st French word was smeared by 50 successive updates.

In 2014 a partial fix appeared: **Bahdanau attention.** Instead of a single postcard, the decoder was now allowed to look back at the encoder's *entire notebook* — every hidden state at every step — and **softly weight** which input footprints to attend to when generating each output footprint. This was the seed of self-attention. It solved problem 1 (information bottleneck) but it was bolted onto an RNN spine that was still sequential, still slow, still forgetful inside its own state.

**The Transformer of 2017 removed the spine entirely.** It said: get rid of the encoder's leather notebook. Get rid of the decoder's leather notebook. Replace both with a shared journal where **every footprint can see every other footprint directly, in one shot, in parallel**. No bottleneck. No forgetting. No sequential walk. The autoregressive *idea* survived. The postcard *did not*.

That is the ache the rest of this manual heals. The cartographer's third crossing — the one that failed for the third time — was seq2seq. The fourth crossing was attention.

**Quick reference — the third crossing's vocabulary:**

| Concept | Cartographer translation | What it actually is | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Seq2Seq** | Two cartographers, two deserts, one postcard between them | RNN encoder + RNN decoder, trained end-to-end | First architecture that mapped variable-length input → variable-length output of a different format |
| **Encoder** | The cartographer who walks the input desert and keeps a running notebook | An RNN/LSTM processing tokens one at a time, updating a hidden state | Compresses the input into a representation the decoder can use |
| **Context vector** | The single postcard mailed at the end of the walk | The encoder's final hidden state — a fixed-size dense vector (e.g. 512 floats) | The *only* channel through which input information reaches the decoder |
| **Fixed size** | The postcard has 4 lines whether the desert was 4 footprints or 4,000 | Hidden-state dimension *d* is baked into the encoder at design time | This *is* the bottleneck — long inputs lose information |
| **Decoder** | The second cartographer in the output desert, holding only the postcard | An RNN/LSTM emitting output tokens conditioned on context + its own previous outputs | Generates the output sequence |
| **Autoregressive decoding** | Each new footprint depends on the postcard + every footprint already pressed | At step *t*, predict $P(y_t \mid y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1}, x)$ — feed previous outputs back in | Captures language dependencies; **the same idea still powers GPT today** |
| **Bahdanau attention (2014)** | The decoder leafs through the encoder's full notebook at every step, not just the postcard | Soft alignment weights over all encoder hidden states, recomputed at every decode step | Killed the bottleneck for the encoder side; first real form of attention |
| **Transformer (2017)** | Replaces both leather notebooks with a single shared journal where every footprint sees every other in parallel | Self-attention everywhere; no recurrence; full parallel computation | Killed the bottleneck *and* the sequential dependency; everything since runs on this |

### The Fourth Crossing — *Attention Is All You Need* (June 2017)

Eight authors at Google Brain published a paper with a title that sounded like a pop song and a result that resembled an architecture-changing event. They threw out the leather notebook. They threw out recurrence. They threw out the postcard. They kept attention — the partial fix from 2014 — and made it the *entire* mechanism. The model now had **no notion of sequence order at all**; positions were added back in via a separate stamp on each footprint (more on that in Component 3).

And the magic of it: **every footprint could now see every other footprint, in one shot, in parallel.** Training became GPU-friendly. Long-range dependencies became cheap. The third-crossing forgetting disappeared.

The rest of this manual is the story of what that one move enabled.

### The Timeline at a Glance

```mermaid
timeline
 title From ELIZA to Modern LLMs
 1966 : ELIZA
 : keyword-pattern bot, no representation
 1990s: n-gram models
 : fixed-window statistics, no long memory
 2014 : Seq2Seq (Sutskever et al.)
 : encoder-decoder LSTM, fixed-size context vector
 2014 : Bahdanau attention
 : decoder peeks at the full encoder notebook
 2017 : Transformer (Attention Is All You Need)
 : self-attention only, parallel, no recurrence
 2018 : BERT
 : bidirectional encoder, masked LM
 2020 : GPT-3 (175B params)
 : decoder-only at scale, in-context learning
 2022 : ChatGPT + RLHF
 : instruction-tuned conversational interface
 2024 : MoE + long context (RoPE, GQA, FlashAttention)
 : trillion-param sparse models, 1M-token windows
 2026 : Multimodal frontier
 : unified text/image/audio/video transformers
```

> **Rest stop.** You now feel the ache. Three previous architectures could each see *some* of the desert, but none could see *all of it without distortion*. The Transformer is the answer to that exact problem. Let's pick up the journal.

---
## Part I — The Seven Gaps Almost Everyone Has

Before we look at any component, we need to fix seven misconceptions that block intuition. Each gap, once closed, makes the rest of the manual feel obvious. **Read each gap twice.** If you read this manual at 2 AM and forget the rest, hold onto these.

### Gap 1 — "Embeddings are the model's knowledge."

Embeddings are the *starting line*, not the destination. An embedding gives you a token's average meaning across all training contexts — what *snow* tends to mean *in general*. By the time the token passes through 32 transformer blocks, that vector has been rewritten dozens of times based on **this specific sentence's** other tokens. Embeddings give you a token's potential. Attention gives you its sentence-specific self.

### Gap 2 — "Self-attention is just weighted averages."

It is, mechanically. But what makes it powerful is that the weights are computed from the tokens themselves, dynamically, every forward pass. Each token *chooses* who to listen to. "The cat sat on the mat and watched **it**" — the word *it* needs to discover, on the fly, that it refers to *the cat*, not *the mat*. No fixed alignment table can do that. Self-attention computes the alignment on the spot.

### Gap 3 — "Context window = how much the model remembers."

Context window = how many tokens the model can attend to *in one forward pass*. That is not the same as memory. The model does not remember anything between forward passes unless you put it back in the prompt. Long context lets the model *see far*; it does not give the model persistence.

### Gap 4 — "More parameters = more knowledge."

More parameters = more *capacity to store and combine* knowledge. Whether the model uses that capacity well depends on data quality, training compute, and architecture choices. GPT-3 is 175B params; LLaMA-2-70B beats it on many benchmarks at less than half the size. **Parameters are a ceiling, not a guarantee.**

### Gap 5 — "Training and inference work the same way."

They do not. **Training** sees the entire ground-truth sequence at once (teacher forcing) and trains all positions in parallel against the next token. **Inference** generates one token at a time, feeds it back in, and uses a KV cache to avoid recomputing what it already computed. The arithmetic is the same; the choreography is completely different. (Part IV.)

### Gap 6 — "The transformer is one block doing magic."

A transformer is a *stack* of identical blocks, typically 12 to 120 of them. Each block does the same two things (attention, then a feed-forward layer), but at different **levels of abstraction**. Layer 1 of a deep model captures local syntax; layer 32 captures discourse-level semantics. Depth is where conceptual hierarchies live.

### Gap 7 — "Generation = the model picking the best next word."

Generation = the model emitting a *probability distribution* over the whole vocabulary, and then a **sampling strategy** picking one word from that distribution. The model rarely "picks" — temperature, top-p, top-k, and beam search are all just rules for rolling the weighted die. Two API calls to the same model with the same prompt and a temperature of 0.7 will often give different outputs. **The sampler is part of the system.**

> **Rest stop.** Seven gaps closed. From here on, the manual assumes you believe each of them. If any feels shaky, re-read just that gap before continuing — they all carry weight ahead.

---
## Part II — The Cartographer's Gear (Inputs)

Before the cartographer can step into the desert, they need three pieces of gear: a way to **press footprints into the sand** (tokenization), a **birth certificate** for each footprint (embedding), and a **clock-stamp** that records where in the journey each footprint was pressed (positional encoding). These three steps happen *before* a single layer of attention runs.

### Component 1 — Tokenization

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A hand pressing numbered footprint stencils into sand, each footprint stamped with an integer ID." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 6 — Tokenization. Raw text is messy; the cartographer presses each meaningful chunk into a discrete, numbered footprint. The model never sees letters; it only ever sees integers.*

Text is a slippery, variable-length, alphabet-soup mess. Models work with tensors of fixed-shape integers. **Tokenization is the bridge** — the gear that takes a string of characters and breaks it into a sequence of discrete chunks ("tokens"), each replaced by an integer ID.

Modern LLMs use **subword tokenizers** (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece). They start from characters and learn — during a pre-processing pass over a huge corpus — which character sequences appear often enough that they deserve their own token. The word *"tokenization"* might become two tokens: *token* + *ization*. The word *"antidisestablishmentarianism"* might become eight. Common words are usually single tokens. Rare words get split into familiar pieces.

**Plain-language summary.** Tokens are the model's atomic units. One token in a modern LLM is roughly ¾ of an English word on average. **"Hello, world!"** is typically 3–4 tokens. The vocabulary is fixed at training time and is usually 30K–200K tokens.

*Why this matters intuitively:* if you ever wonder why an LLM stumbles on rare proper names or unusual code identifiers, this is why. The tokenizer chopped them into unfamiliar fragments and the model is reasoning about *foo*, *_bar_*, *_42* — not about your variable name.

### Component 2 — Embedding

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A large open ledger on a dune; each row lists a word and its multi-dimensional vector — the master ledger of embeddings." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 7 — The master ledger. Every token ID indexes into the embedding table to retrieve a dense vector — the token's birth certificate. Same ID → same starting vector, every time.*

Once we have integer IDs, we need to give each one a **rich, learnable identity** in a high-dimensional space. That is what the embedding table does: it is a giant lookup table with one row per vocabulary token. Row 1839 contains the 12,288-dimensional vector that *is* the meaning of token 1839 (in GPT-3.5's case).

**Plain-language summary.** An embedding is a dense vector (typically 256–12,288 floats) that captures the token's *prior* meaning — what it tends to mean across all training contexts. Words that mean similar things end up with vectors pointing in similar directions: *cat* and *dog* sit close together; *cat* and *skateboard* sit far apart.

**Cartographer's translation.** Every footprint shape gets a **birth certificate** filed in the master ledger (Figure 7). When you re-encounter the same footprint shape later in the desert, you flip to the same page and copy out the same starting vector.

**Critical caveat — this is Gap 1 in action.** The embedding is the *starting point*, not the answer. It is what *snow* means before the model has read the rest of the sentence. By the time the token has flowed through 32 transformer blocks, that 12,288-vector has been rewritten dozens of times by attention and the FFN. Layer 1's representation of *cat* looks like a fuzzy *cat archetype*. Layer 32's representation of *cat* in the sentence *"the specific black cat that ran across the street"* looks like a context-specific encoding of *that particular cat*. **Same starting row in the ledger. Wildly different vector at the exit.**

### Component 3 — Positional Encoding

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A branding iron stamping clock-faces onto a row of footprints; each footprint shows its position." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 8 — Positional encoding. Self-attention treats inputs as an unordered set. A clock-stamp is branded onto each embedding so the model knows where each footprint lives in the desert.*

Here we hit one of the most counter-intuitive facts about transformers: **self-attention has no built-in notion of order.** If you shuffle the input tokens, you get the same set of attention weights (just permuted). That is a disaster for language, where *"dog bites man"* and *"man bites dog"* are very different sentences.

**The fix:** before the embeddings flow into the first attention layer, we *add* a positional encoding vector to each one — a deterministic or learned vector that depends only on the position (1, 2, 3, …). Now token 5 carries both *what it is* and *where it sits*.

Modern variants include:
- **Sinusoidal** (original 2017 paper) — fixed sin/cos of varying frequencies, no learned parameters.
- **Learned absolute** — one trainable vector per position up to context-window length.
- **RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding)** — rotates the Q and K vectors based on position, used in LLaMA, GPT-NeoX, modern models. Encodes *relative* position naturally and extrapolates better to longer sequences.
- **ALiBi** — adds a position-dependent bias directly to attention scores. Simple and effective at extending context length.

**Cartographer's translation.** Without positional encoding, the cartographer's journal would have a list of footprints with no information about *when* each was pressed. The branding iron stamps a clock-face onto each one so the chronology is preserved.

> **Rest stop.** Gear check: footprints pressed (tokens), birth certificates issued (embeddings), clock-faces stamped (positional encoding). The cartographer is now standing at the edge of the desert with everything they need. Time to walk.

---
## Part III — The Council of Scouts (the Transformer Block)

Every transformer block does the same two things in sequence: **(1) talk across tokens** (attention), then **(2) think locally per token** (a feed-forward network). Both operations are wrapped in residual connections and layer normalization, which are what make deep networks of these blocks actually trainable. We'll walk through each piece.

### Component 4 — Self-Attention (the heart of it all)

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A row of footprints labeled 'The cat sat on the mat and watched it'. The last footprint 'it' glows and sends colored beams of varying thickness back to earlier footprints — strongest to 'cat'." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 9 — Self-attention. The focal token "it" dispatches scouts to every earlier footprint to ask 'how relevant are you to me?'. Thicker beam = higher attention weight. The token is then rewritten as the weighted blend of the values it attended to.*

This is the component that, more than any other, makes the Transformer what it is. Read it twice.

**The intuition.** For every token in the input, self-attention does three things:

1. The token asks a *question*: "what kind of context do I need?" (the **query**, Q)
2. Every other token offers a *label*: "here's what I am" (the **key**, K)
3. Every other token also offers a *payload*: "here's what I'll contribute" (the **value**, V)

The token compares its question to every label (the **dot product Q·K**), gets a score for each, normalizes those scores into a probability distribution (the **softmax**), and then takes a weighted sum of all the payloads. **The token has rewritten itself as a blend of every other token's contribution, weighted by relevance.**

**Under the hood, the matrix view.** For a sequence of *N* tokens, each represented as a *d*-dimensional vector:

1. **Project** the input matrix `X` (shape `N × d`) into three matrices `Q`, `K`, `V`, each shape `N × d`, using three learned weight matrices `W_Q`, `W_K`, `W_V`.
2. **Score** every query against every key: compute `S = Q · K^T`, shape `N × N`. Entry `(i, j)` says how much token *i* wants to listen to token *j*.
3. **Normalize** each row of `S` into a probability distribution: `A = softmax(S / √d)`. The √d divisor stops scores from blowing up at high dimensions.
4. **Mix** the values according to those weights: `Z = A · V`, shape `N × d`. Each row of `Z` is the rewritten representation of the corresponding input token.

**The killer property.** This computation is **fully parallel** across all *N* tokens. There is no recurrence. Every token's new representation is computed at the same time as every other token's. That is the entire reason transformers train so well on GPUs.

### Component 4b — A Worked Example: *who is snow white* vs *why is snow white*

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Two rows of footprints showing the same word 'snow' attending differently in two sentences." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 10 — Same token, different sentence-self. In "who is snow white", the word 'snow' attends strongly to 'who' and gets pulled toward the proper-noun interpretation (the Disney character). In "why is snow white", the same starting embedding for 'snow' attends differently, and the hidden state at the exit encodes the natural-phenomenon meaning.*

Consider two sentences that share the same three words: **"who is snow white"** and **"why is snow white"**. The token *snow* enters with the same embedding both times — same row of the ledger. After one pass of self-attention, those two *snows* have wildly different vectors:

- In *who is snow white*, the question-word **who** signals "we're talking about a person." *Snow*'s attention pulls strongly from *who* and pushes its vector toward the *Snow White (Disney character)* region of representation space.
- In *why is snow white*, the question-word **why** signals "we're asking about a property." *Snow*'s attention pulls differently, and the vector tilts toward the *frozen-precipitation* region.

**Same embedding in. Different hidden state out.** That is Gap 1 made concrete — and Gap 2 made concrete: the attention weights are not fixed alignments, they are computed on the fly from the actual tokens present. This is also why the transformer can disambiguate pronouns like *it* in *"The cat sat on the mat and watched **it**"* — *it* asks who it could be referring to, listens hardest to *cat*, and rewrites itself accordingly.

### Component 5 — Multi-Head Attention

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A central footprint surrounded by a ring of 8 colored scouts, each labeled with a different specialization." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 11 — Multi-head attention. Instead of one big scout, the cartographer dispatches H smaller scouts in parallel, each watching a different kind of relationship.*

One self-attention is good. **H of them, in parallel, watching different things — is much better.** That is multi-head attention.

Concretely: instead of projecting into one `Q`, `K`, `V` of dimension `d`, we project into `H` smaller sets, each of dimension `d/H`. We run `H` independent self-attentions in parallel, then concatenate the results and pass them through one more linear projection.

**Why this helps:** different heads learn to specialize. Inspect a trained model and you will find one head that tracks **syntactic dependencies** (verb agrees with subject), one that tracks **coreference** (which *it* refers to which noun), one that tracks **positional patterns** (this is the first token in the sentence), one that tracks **rare words**, and so on. **The council, not the lone scout, is what gives the transformer its sophistication.**

GPT-3.5 has 96 heads per layer. LLaMA-2-70B has 64. The number is a hyperparameter chosen by the architect.

### Component 6 — Causal Mask (the glass wall)

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A row of footprints; one in the middle glows; a translucent vertical glass wall blocks vision to the right, dimming all future footprints." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 12 — Causal masking. In a generative model, when the cartographer is at footprint t, a glass wall prevents them from peeking at footprints t+1, t+2, ... — they may only attend to the past.*

In a decoder-only model (GPT, LLaMA, etc.) we train by **predicting each token from its predecessors only**. If position 5 could attend to position 6, the model would just copy the answer and learn nothing. The fix is the **causal mask**: before softmax, we set every "future" attention score to negative infinity, so after softmax their weight becomes zero.

**Cartographer's translation.** A glass wall drops down between the present footprint and every footprint to its right. The cartographer may look back as far as the desert allows, but never forward.

**Why this is one of the most consequential design choices.** It is what makes a transformer *generative*. Without it, training and inference would not be aligned. With it, you can train the model on every position in parallel (each one tries to predict the next, all at once), and then at inference you generate one token at a time and the masking guarantees the model never sees the future. **Causal masking is the bridge between training efficiency and autoregressive generation** — the very property that survived from the seq2seq era.

### Component 7 — Residuals and LayerNorm

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="An open journal with margin annotations in red, sitting under a recalibrated ruler." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 13 — Residuals + LayerNorm. Attention's output is added to the input (residual connection), not used to replace it. Then the result is rescaled so the next layer can read it without arithmetic drift.*

Two unglamorous pieces of plumbing without which deep transformers don't train at all.

**Residual connection:** instead of replacing the input `x` with the attention output `Attn(x)`, we *add* them: `x → x + Attn(x)`. The model now learns the *delta*, the **correction**, not the full output. This makes gradients flow cleanly through dozens of layers (without residuals, deep networks suffer from vanishing/exploding gradients).

**LayerNorm (or RMSNorm in modern models):** rescales each token's vector so its mean is 0 and standard deviation is 1, independent of the others. This stops activation magnitudes from drifting wildly between layers and keeps the optimizer happy.

**Cartographer's translation.** The cartographer never *erases* the journal entries from previous layers. Every block adds its corrections as margin annotations (residual). Then the ruler at the top of the page is recalibrated (LayerNorm) so the next block can read the page cleanly.

**Pre-norm vs post-norm.** Original 2017 paper put LayerNorm *after* attention. Modern models (GPT-2, LLaMA, etc.) put it *before*. Pre-norm trains more stably at scale. It is a small detail with a large empirical effect.

### Component 8 — Feed-Forward Network

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A lit tent under a starry constellation; lines from each star to the tent suggest information being pulled in and processed." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 14 — The feed-forward network. After the scouts return from their conversations across the desert, the cartographer ducks into a lit tent and quietly thinks about what each footprint has just learned.*

Attention let the tokens *talk*. The FFN lets each token *think* — independently, in private, with no further cross-token communication.

Concretely, the FFN is a simple two-layer MLP applied to each token's vector individually:

```
x → Linear(d, 4d) → GELU → Linear(4d, d)
```

Two facts that are easy to miss:

1. **The hidden dimension is 4×** the model dimension. In GPT-3.5 that means a 12,288-dim input expands to a 49,152-dim hidden vector and contracts back. That's a *lot* of compute per token.
2. **This is where most of the model's parameters live.** In GPT-3.5, FFNs hold **66%** of all 175 billion weights. The cartographer is, by parameter count, mostly tent. (Part VII shows the breakdown.)

**Why the 4× expansion?** Intuition: attention has already mixed the right context into each token. The FFN's job is to do *non-linear feature transformation* on that mixed context — to query a large "knowledge bank" stored in its weights for whatever's relevant. The expansion gives that knowledge bank enough room to be expressive.

### Component 9 — Stacking N Blocks

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A horizon of identical tents at increasing heights, with stacks of pages growing thicker beside each one — the journal thickens with depth." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 15 — Stacking. One block builds local relationships. N stacked blocks build hierarchical, abstract relationships layer by layer.*

A single transformer block is interesting. **N identical blocks stacked vertically** is what makes the model powerful. Each layer reads the previous layer's output and refines it further.

**The depth pattern.** Early layers handle syntactic and local features (this is a noun, this verb agrees with that subject). Middle layers handle medium-range semantics (this clause modifies that one). Late layers handle long-range, abstract relationships (this whole paragraph is sarcastic, this code block has a subtle off-by-one bug).

Typical depths:
- Small models: 6–12 layers (GPT-2 small, BERT-base).
- Mid-size: 24–48 layers (BERT-large, GPT-2 large).
- Frontier: 60–120 layers (GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2-70B, etc.).

### Component 10 — KV Cache (the trick that makes inference cheap)

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A massive half-buried ledger with rows of K and V entries already filled in; a new glowing entry is being added at the bottom." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 16 — KV cache. During autoregressive generation, the cartographer keeps the K and V vectors for every previous footprint in a ledger. At each new step, only the new footprint's K and V are computed; everything else is looked up.*

Here is where autoregressive inference would explode without a clever trick.

Naive autoregressive generation: at step *t*, recompute self-attention from scratch over all *t* tokens. Step 1: 1 token. Step 2: 2 tokens. Step *t*: *t* tokens. Total work over a 1000-token generation: about 500,000 token-steps. **Wasteful.**

**The insight:** when generating token *t+1*, the K and V vectors for tokens 1…*t* are *exactly the same* as they were when generating token *t*. We already computed them. Why throw them away?

**The fix:** maintain a **KV cache** — a per-layer, per-head ledger of every K and V vector ever computed in this generation. At each new step, compute K and V only for the *single new token* and append. Compute the new Q. Run attention against the entire cache. Done.

This turns generation from quadratic to linear in the number of tokens, and is what makes ChatGPT-style streaming responses possible.

**The cost:** the KV cache is *big*. For a model with `L` layers and `d` model-dim, each step adds roughly `2 · L · d` floats per token to the cache. A 70B model generating 8K tokens can need many gigabytes of GPU memory just for the KV cache. **This is the bottleneck of long-context inference**, and the reason for a whole industry of optimizations (PagedAttention, GQA, quantized KV caches, etc.).

### Component 11 — Unembedding

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A wide horizon of variable-height lighthouses, two of which are markedly taller, labeled 'cat' and 'dog'." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 17 — Unembedding. After the final block, each token's d-dim vector is projected back into a |V|-dim vector of logits — one per vocabulary word. The vocabulary becomes a horizon of lighthouses; the tallest are the most likely next words.*

After *N* blocks of work, each token has a final *d*-dimensional representation. To pick the next word, we project that vector back into the vocabulary space. The output is a vector of length *|V|* (the vocabulary size, e.g. 50,257), one **logit** per vocabulary word.

**Trick:** the unembedding matrix is often *tied* to the embedding matrix — same weights, transposed. This saves parameters and tends to improve training (the mapping from vocab→vector and vector→vocab should be consistent).

**Cartographer's translation.** The journal's last page is now compared against every entry in the master ledger. The result is a horizon of variable-height lighthouses — one per vocabulary word. **Lighthouse height = how strongly the model thinks that word is the next footprint.** — Softmax

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A pie chart drawn in the sand showing probability slices for 'cat', 'dog', 'hat', 'ran', '…', alongside logit-to-probability annotations." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 18 — Softmax. Raw lighthouse heights (logits) are turned into a clean probability pie. The exponential makes confident-looking logits dominate; the normalization makes the slices sum to 1.*

Lighthouse heights (logits) are real numbers — possibly negative, possibly enormous. To use them as a sampling distribution, we need them to be probabilities (non-negative, summing to 1). That is what softmax does:

$$\text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i / T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j / T}}$$

The exponential amplifies confident logits (a logit of 5 becomes much bigger than a logit of 3). The normalization makes the result a proper probability distribution. The *T* (temperature) is a knob that controls sharpness — more on that in Component 13.

### Component 13 — Sampling

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A weighted die mid-tumble above a bar chart showing 'cat' 58%, 'dog' 18%, 'hat' 12%, 'ran' 7%, '(others)' 5%." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 19 — Sampling. Once we have a probability distribution over the next word, we still need to pick one. Sampling is the rule that picks. Greedy always picks the tallest bar; temperature/top-p/top-k each bias the die differently.*

**This is Gap 7.** The model emits a *distribution*. The **sampling strategy** picks one word from that distribution. The same model + prompt with two different samplers will produce very different outputs.

**The main strategies:**

- **Greedy:** always pick the highest-probability word. Deterministic, but tends to produce repetitive, robotic text.
- **Temperature:** divide the logits by *T* before softmax. `T < 1` sharpens the distribution (more deterministic). `T > 1` flattens it (more random).
- **Top-k:** restrict sampling to the top *k* highest-probability words, then sample within those.
- **Top-p (nucleus):** restrict sampling to the smallest set of words whose cumulative probability exceeds *p* (e.g. 0.9). Adaptive — keeps lots of options when the model is uncertain, few when it's confident.
- **Beam search:** maintain *b* parallel candidate sequences, score each, keep the best. Used in translation; rarely used for free-form generation (tends to produce bland outputs).

#### The Sweet Spot — Temperature × Top-p

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A 2x2 quadrant chart: low-T low-p (RIGID), low-T high-p (PRECISE ), high-T low-p (VOLATILE), high-T high-p (CHAOTIC)." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 20 — Production sampling sweet spot. The interaction between temperature and top-p matters more than either alone. Most well-tuned generation lives in the upper-left quadrant: low temperature for coherence, high top-p to keep enough options for diversity.*

In practice, temperature and top-p are not independent knobs — their *interaction* defines four operating regimes (Figure 20):

- **RIGID** (low T, low p): deterministic, brittle, often loops or repeats.
- **PRECISE ** (low T, high p): focused but flexible — the usual production setting. Most chat models default to roughly *T = 0.7, top-p = 0.9*.
- **VOLATILE** (high T, low p): random within a narrow set — produces weird-but-confined outputs.
- **CHAOTIC** (high T, high p): often incoherent. Useful only for creative brainstorming.

> **Rest stop.** That is the complete inventory of the cartographer's gear and council. **Tokenize → Embed → +PE → (Attention → FFN) × N → Unembed → Softmax → Sample.** Every modern LLM is a variation on that pattern. We're ready to look at the full crossing.

## Part IV — Two Modes (Training vs. Inference)

**This is Gap 5.** Training and inference share the same forward pass, but they orchestrate it very differently. Knowing the difference is one of the clearest signals that you really understand what a transformer is.

### Training — Teacher Forcing in Parallel

During training, the model sees the entire ground-truth sequence at once. To train it to predict the next token, we feed in tokens 1…N and ask it to predict tokens 2…N+1, all positions in parallel. The causal mask (Component 6) ensures position *i* can only attend to positions 1…*i*. We compute the cross-entropy loss between the model's predictions and the actual next tokens, sum it across the sequence, and backpropagate.

**This is called teacher forcing.** Even if the model would have predicted the wrong word at position 5, we still show it the *true* word at position 5 when computing the loss at position 6. The model never gets to walk into its own errors during training — it always sees a correct prefix.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
 A["full sequence<br/>tokens 1..N"] --> B["one forward pass<br/>all positions parallel"]
 B --> C["next-token loss<br/>at every position"]
 C --> D["backprop<br/>update all weights"]
 D --> A
```

### Inference — One Footprint at a Time

Inference is autoregressive — exactly the choreography we met in Part 0 with the seq2seq decoder, except now there is no postcard. The model has full direct attention over every previous token via the KV cache.

The loop:

1. Start with the prompt tokens (the **prefill** phase: one big forward pass over the whole prompt, populating the KV cache).
2. Compute the logits for the next token (the **decode** step).
3. Apply softmax and the sampling strategy to pick a token.
4. Append the chosen token to the input. Add its K and V to the cache.
5. Forward-pass *only the new token* through the model (the cache provides everything else).
6. Repeat from step 2 until `<EOS>` or max-length.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
 P["prompt tokens"] --> PF["PREFILL<br/>one big pass"]
 PF --> KV[("KV cache")]
 KV --> DG["DECODE<br/>one token at a time"]
 DG --> S["sample next token"]
 S --> APP["append to KV cache"]
 APP --> DG
 S --> OUT["streamed output"]
```

**Two regimes, two bottlenecks.** Prefill is *compute-bound* (one big matmul over the entire prompt). Decode is *memory-bound* (you read the entire KV cache from HBM for every single token). This split is the reason latency profiling of LLMs talks about *time-to-first-token* (prefill) and *time-per-output-token* (decode) as two separate numbers.

---
## Part V — The Architecture Family

The 2017 paper described an encoder-decoder transformer (for translation). The field has since explored three flavors of the same skeleton.

| Flavor | Examples | Attention pattern | Best at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Encoder-only** | BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa | Bidirectional (no mask) | Classification, embeddings, sentence understanding |
| **Decoder-only** | GPT family, LLaMA, Claude, Mistral | Causal (masked) | Text generation, code, modern chat assistants |
| **Encoder-decoder** | T5, BART, original 2017 model | Encoder bidirectional + decoder causal + cross-attention | Translation, summarization, structured input→output |

**Why decoder-only dominates modern chat:** it is the cleanest fit for the *autoregressive* objective we inherited from seq2seq (Part 0). One model. One loss. One inference loop. Scales beautifully. Everything you ask it to do can be framed as "continue this conversation."

**Why encoder-only is still everywhere in production:** when all you need is to *understand* a document (classify it, embed it, search it), the bidirectional attention of BERT-style models is more efficient than running a generative model and reading its outputs.

**Why encoder-decoder still wins for translation:** translation is fundamentally a *transduction* task — variable-length input in one format, variable-length output in another. The encoder-decoder split (with cross-attention as the bridge) is a more natural fit than a single causal stream. T5 elegantly framed *every* NLP task as text-to-text, and that paradigm is what eventually evolved into modern multi-task instruction tuning.

## Part VI — The Full Crossing

You now know each piece of the cartographer's gear and every member of the council of scouts. **Now we bring it all together — the entire crossing in one view, from the moment you press *enter* to the moment the model prints a token, and the loop that does it again.**

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A horizontal flowchart with eight stages — Text → Tokens → Embed → +PE → Block ×N → Unembed → Softmax → Sample — with a red autoregressive loop arching from Sample back to Tokens. Below the boxes, a note about KV cache reuse." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 21 — The full crossing. Eight stages from text to next token, plus the autoregressive loop that turns one prediction into a stream. The very same loop that the seq2seq decoder used in 2014 — except now there is no postcard, and every previous token can be attended to directly via the KV cache.*

The journey, in one paragraph: when you type a prompt, the tokenizer presses each chunk into a numbered footprint. The embedding table issues a birth-certificate vector for each one. The positional encoder stamps a clock-face. The first transformer block then dispatches its multi-head council of scouts; each scout reads every other footprint and reports back. The block's tent (FFN) thinks about what the scouts found, and the residual + LayerNorm machinery wraps the journal page cleanly. *That same process repeats N times.* By the final layer, the vector for the last token has been rewritten dozens of times based on the full context. The unembedding matrix projects it back into vocabulary space — a horizon of lighthouses, one per word. Softmax turns those lighthouse heights into a probability pie. The sampler rolls a weighted die over that pie and picks the next token. The new token's K and V vectors get filed in the cache. The cartographer is back at the start of the loop — except now the desert has one more footprint than before. **That's it. That's the whole machine.**

---
## Part VII — Case Study: GPT-3.5 (175 Billion Parameters)

With the full journey traced, let's pause and walk one specific desert end-to-end on the map. **GPT-3.5 has 175,181,291,520 parameters.** That sounds enormous — and it is — but the structure we built up in Parts II and III tells you *exactly* where each one lives. The interesting question is not how many there are, but **which item in the cartographer's bag is actually heaviest.**

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Bar chart titled 'GPT-3.5 — Where the 175 Billion Weights Live': FFN (the tents) 115.8B / 66%, Self-Attention (scouts) 41.6B / 24%, Embedding (ledger) <1%, Unembedding (lighthouses) <1%, Other ~9%." style="width:100%;max-width:1100px;display:block;margin:14px 0;" />
*Figure 22 — GPT-3.5's parameter inventory. Two-thirds of the weights live in the FFN tents. The scouts (attention) hold most of the rest. The ledger and lighthouses combined cost less than 1%. The cartographer, by weight, is mostly tent.*

### The Specs

| Spec | Value | Cartographer translation |
|---|---|---|
| Layers (depth) | 96 | The journal has 96 marginal-annotation rounds |
| `d_model` | 12,288 | Each footprint's vector is 12,288 floats |
| Heads per layer | 96 | 96 scouts dispatch per layer, each watching one kind of pattern |
| Head dimension | 128 | Each scout's question/label/payload is 128 floats |
| FFN hidden dimension | 49,152 (4× `d_model`) | The tent has 49K thinking-slots per token per layer |
| Vocabulary size | 50,257 | 50K possible lighthouses on the horizon |
| Context window | 4,096 tokens (original) | Up to ~4K footprints visible at once |
| Total parameters | **175,181,291,520** | |

### Where the Weights Actually Live

The bar chart above (Figure 22) gives the headline. The detailed accounting:

- **FFN tents — 115.8 B parameters (66%).** Two weight matrices per layer of shape `d × 4d = 12,288 × 49,152`. Per layer: about 1.2 billion params. Times 96 layers = ~115.8 B. **This is where the model's factual knowledge primarily lives** — most of what GPT-3.5 "knows" about the world is encoded in these tent walls.
- **Self-Attention scouts — 41.6 B parameters (24%).** Four projection matrices per layer (W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O), each of shape `d × d = 12,288 × 12,288`. Per layer: about 600 million params (with bias). Times 96 layers = ~41.6 B. **This is where the model's contextual routing lives** — the rules for who-listens-to-whom.
- **Embedding ledger — ~0.62 B parameters (<1%).** One vector per vocabulary word, each of dimension `d`. 50,257 × 12,288 ≈ 620 million.
- **Unembedding lighthouses — ~0.62 B (<1%).** Same shape as the embedding table. Often weight-tied (shared with embeddings) in modern models; GPT-3 kept them separate.
- **Other (LayerNorm scales/biases, attention biases, etc.) — ~16 B (~9%).** Tiny per-tensor but they add up across 96 layers.

**The single takeaway:** if you cared only about *where the cartographer carries weight*, you would point at the tents. **Most of the model is FFN.** That fact has direct engineering consequences. When people talk about model-distillation, low-rank-adaptation (LoRA), or mixture-of-experts (MoE), they are nearly always operating on the FFN. The scouts and the ledger are too small to compress meaningfully; the tents are where the savings are.

> **Rest stop.** Case study landed. **The cartographer is mostly tent**, and now you know exactly why — and what that implies for distillation, quantization, MoE, and the whole optimization industry that has grown up around making these models cheaper to run.

## Part VIII — The Decoder Ring (Quick Reference)

If you need to find one fact fast, this is the table.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What's the input to the model? | A sequence of token IDs (integers) of length ≤ context window. |
| What's the output of one forward pass? | A `(N × |V|)` matrix of logits — one row per input position, one column per vocabulary word. |
| What gets sampled? | Only the **last** row of logits (the prediction for the position right after the last input token). |
| Why do we add positional encoding? | Self-attention is permutation-invariant; without PE, *"dog bites man"* and *"man bites dog"* are identical. |
| Why divide attention scores by √d? | Without it, dot products grow with `d` and softmax saturates, killing gradients. |
| Why multi-head? | Different heads specialize on different kinds of relationships (syntax, coreference, position, …). |
| What does the causal mask do? | Sets future-attention scores to `-∞` so they become 0 after softmax. |
| What does the residual connection do? | Lets gradients flow cleanly through deep stacks; lets each block learn a *delta*. |
| What does LayerNorm do? | Normalizes each token's vector to zero mean / unit variance per layer; stops magnitudes from drifting. |
| Where do most parameters live? | The FFN (≈ 2/3 of all weights in a typical decoder-only model). |
| What's the KV cache? | A per-layer/per-head ledger of K and V from earlier decode steps; avoids recomputation. |
| What's teacher forcing? | During training, feeding the true previous tokens (not the model's predictions) when computing the next-token loss. |
| Why is decoding sequential but training parallel? | Causal mask makes both possible; training has the answers up front, decoding does not. |
| What's autoregressive generation? | Predicting one token, appending it to the input, predicting the next, looping. |
| What's a context vector (seq2seq)? | A fixed-size dense vector summarizing the whole input; the seq2seq bottleneck. Transformers do not have one. |

---
## Appendix A — The ABBA Paradox (a stress test for your intuition)

Here is a puzzle that breaks naive intuition about attention. Consider the input:

> *"A B B A"*

Self-attention is permutation-invariant in its raw form (recall Component 3). Positional encoding fixes that. **But:** what if we encode positions using *relative* positions only (like RoPE), and the model is being asked to distinguish *"A B B A"* from *"B A A B"*?

Each token is identical in vocabulary. The bigram-level statistics — what tokens appear adjacent to what — are *also* identical (A→B, B→B, B→A vs. B→A, A→A, A→B). The only way to tell these two sequences apart is to use *absolute* position or to attend to the full pattern of the sequence, not just local neighbors.

**Why this matters:** it shows that simple positional schemes have failure modes, and it's part of why modern models combine RoPE (great at relative position generalization) with other tricks (interpolation, longer-context fine-tuning) to handle truly long-range patterns. **The desert can be subtle. The cartographer's clock-stamp matters as much as the footprints.**

## Appendix B — Reading Order If You Want to Go Deeper

Once you've internalized this manual, here is the curriculum that builds on it:

1. **"Attention Is All You Need"** (Vaswani et al., 2017) — read it now, having walked the desert. It will feel obvious.
2. **The Illustrated Transformer** (Jay Alammar) — best free visual companion.
3. **The Annotated Transformer** (Harvard NLP) — paper + working PyTorch line by line.
4. **BERT paper** (Devlin et al., 2018) — encoder-only, bidirectional. Read after.
5. **GPT-3 paper** ("Language Models are Few-Shot Learners", Brown et al., 2020) — what scale reveals.
6. **RoPE paper** (Su et al., 2021) — modern positional encoding.
7. **FlashAttention** (Dao et al., 2022) — the attention-kernel breakthrough.
8. **Chinchilla paper** (Hoffmann et al., 2022) — the scaling-law correction.
9. **LLaMA papers** (Touvron et al., 2023) — modern decoder-only design choices.
10. **Mixtral / MoE papers** — where the FFN tents got split into experts.

## Coda — One Last Walk

Five crossings have happened. ELIZA shouted at a wall. The n-gram cartographer carried a sliding window with hard edges. The RNN cartographer carried a leather notebook that smeared at the end. The seq2seq cartographer mailed a fixed-size postcard that lost the early chapters. The Transformer threw out the spine and replaced it with a shared journal where every footprint can see every other.

**The desert never changed. Only the cartographer's gear did.**

If you remember nothing else, remember this: *every token enters the journal as its embedding-prior, and every layer rewrites it slightly based on its sentence-specific neighbors, until — at the final page — it is no longer the dictionary word. It is **that word, here, now, in this sentence.*** That's what the model knows. That's what the model is.

Walk well.
